newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan's Mr Yen causes turbulence in markets.
newsitem.headline: Japan's Mr Yen causes turbulence in markets.

text.p: The bouncing dollar rose more than four yen in Tokyo trade on Thursday as Japanese officials sent out urgent signals that the nation's trade surplus was not a major issue and an interest rate rise was not imminent.

Senior Finance Ministry official Eisuke Sakakibara, dubbed "Mr. Yen" for his influence on exchange rates, was again the oracle who sent markets into a spin with a raft of comments on currencies, interest rates and the trade balance.
Sakakibara told reporters that the Japanese government was resolved to prevent any excessive swings in foreign exchange markets, where the yen has been on a rising trend.
The remarks boosted the dollar to nearly 116 yen, compared with 111.29 yen in late U.S. trade on Wednesday and a seven-month low of 110.62 yen hit earlier that day in London.
The dollar, which was over 120 yen just last month, was hovering around 112 yen when the Tokyo market opened.

"The prime minister has instructed us to act against forex moves in a timely and appropriate manner. We will act decisively against excessive forex moves," Sakakibara told reporters after giving a speech at a financial seminar in Tokyo.
Predictably, Tokyo stock prices shot higher in afternoon trade as the yen fell sharply against the dollar.
A strong yen makes Japanese products more expensive in global markets, hurting the profits in yen terms of Japanese exporters, the backbone of the country's economy.
The yen had been rising against the dollar since early May amid growing fears that a rebound in Japan's trade surplus could revive trade friction with the United States.
It had also been helped by expectations that Japan's minimal interest rates might be on the way up soon.

Sakakibara cast doubt on those expectations with comments ruling out an imminent interest rate rise, which also sent bond prices higher. The comments were made in a speech to the seminar and relayed to reporters later by seminar participants.
Former Vice Finance Minister Tomomitsu Oba, who attended the seminar, told reporters Sakakibara may think a yen rate slightly stronger than 120 yen to the dollar is an appropriate level.

Sakakibara also said he did not think Japan's trade surplus is a major concern, and that it is unlikely to be a major issue at a summit meeting of the Group of Seven industrial nations in Denver from June 20-22.

The Yomiuri Shimbun reported on Thursday morning, quoting Japanese government sources, that the G7 leaders will urge Japan to reduce its trade surplus and push forward with economic structural reform.
